rows.R: Protocol v5.0 p43 (10.1.1): painTRAINER sessions take 45-60 min; p44 (10.1.2): coach sessions take 60 min. Main p3 and TIDieR supp3 pp3-4: painTRAINER 30-45 min, coach 45-60 min. Session number (8) and 12-week window unchanged. Described per-session dose is shorter in the report for both arms (non-overlapping for painTRAINER); may reflect a revised completion-time estimate rather than changed content. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Main p3 (text); protocol supp1 pp43-44 (text layer encoded; OCR at 300 dpi and 110-dpi renders read visually); TIDieR supp3 pp3-4 (text). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The protocol describes each online painTRAINER session as taking 45-60 minutes and each coach session as 60 minutes. The article and the TIDieR supplement describe painTRAINER sessions as 30-45 minutes and coach sessions as 45-60 minutes. The number of sessions, weekly cadence and 12-week completion window are the same. For painTRAINER the two ranges do not overlap; for the coach arm the reported range extends below the planned fixed length. This is a difference in the described intervention procedure (contact time per session), which affects extraction of intervention dose (8 x 45-60 = 6-8 h planned vs 8 x 30-45 = 4-6 h reported for painTRAINER). Neither document says whether the figures are design estimates or observed times, and the self-paced program content may be unchanged, so the difference is descriptive only. Coded substantive_difference because the per-session dose description differs for both arms; another reviewer could reasonably treat it as minor_presentation.

rows.R: Main p4: painTRAINER '371 (43%) completed at least 6 sessions'. Figure 1 p5: 776 randomized; 371 + 156 + 249 = 776. 371/776 = 47.8% (printed 43%); 371/527 initiators = 70.4%. Other three adherence percentages reproduce (527/776 = 67.9%, 660/778 = 84.8%, 548/778 = 70.4%). Count is correct, percentage wrong. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Main pp4-5 (text; Figure 1 flow counts from text layer). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: Text: 'Of those randomized to the painTRAINER group, 527 (68%) completed at least 1 session and 371 (43%) completed at least 6 sessions (therapeutic dose).' Figure 1 gives 776 randomized to painTRAINER with 371 completing 6-8 sessions, 156 completing 1-5 and 249 none (sum 776). Recomputed: 371/776 = 0.478 (47.8%); 527/776 = 67.9% (printed 68%, correct). The parallel health coach figures reproduce (660/778 = 84.8% printed 85%; 548/778 = 70.4% printed 70%). No denominator gives 43%: 371/527 = 70.4%; 371/863 would be needed. The count and denominator are printed, so the correct value is recoverable, and the qualitative point (lower adherence with painTRAINER) is unchanged, although the gap to health coach is overstated (43% vs 70% printed; 48% vs 70% correct). Confirmed, minor_presentation; downstream possible because adherence percentages are commonly extracted.

rows.R: Main p4 and Table 3 note d (p11): SMD = adjusted MD / SD of UC change at that time point, so the three contrasts at a time point share one denominator. Recomputed for all 21 rows: implied SD (MD/SMD) differs across the three columns of one row (e.g., social 3 mo: 6.7, 150, 3.5), 4 SMDs have the opposite sign to their MD, HC-PT SMD is -0.08 to -0.13 where MD is 0.0, and SMD(HC-PT) is not SMD(HC-UC) - SMD(PT-UC) in 17 rows. SMD columns cannot follow the stated definition. Also: text p7 quotes 3-month SMDs -0.26/-0.36, which are the 6-month values in Table 3 (3-month: -0.25/-0.34). Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Main pp4, 7, 10-11 (text layer; Table 3 checked against the rendered page). R script smd.R in working folder. Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: Footnote d and the methods define the SMD as the adjusted between-group mean difference divided by the SD of change in the usual care plus group at the given time point. Under this definition all three contrasts at one outcome/time share one positive denominator, so (i) MD/SMD must be constant across the three columns, (ii) the SMD must have the sign of its MD, and (iii) SMD(HC-PT) = SMD(HC-UC) - SMD(PT-UC). Recomputation over all 21 outcome/time rows (63 tuples): implied SD varies within row far beyond rounding (pain severity 3 mo 1.60, 1.18, and 0 for HC-PT where MD = -0.0 but SMD = -0.13; social role 3 mo 6.7, 150, 3.5; PGIC pain 3 mo 1.13, 1.45, 0.54); sign conflicts in 4 tuples (physical 3 mo HC-UC MD +0.7 vs SMD -0.02; physical 6 mo HC-PT -0.3 vs +0.22; physical 12 mo HC-PT -0.1 vs +0.27; PGIC pain 12 mo HC-PT +0.1 vs -0.29); additivity fails in most rows (social 3 mo 0.12/0.01/0.20; physical 6 mo 0.15/0.02/0.22). For the social and physical rows the SMD pattern looks as if the HC-UC and HC-PT columns were exchanged or shifted, but no single permutation reconciles all rows, so the intended values cannot be recovered. The 14 out-of-interval points (C010) and 18 reversed intervals are further manifestations. In addition, the Results text (p7) quotes 3-month SMDs of -0.26 (painTRAINER) and -0.36 (health coach), which are the 6-month values in Table 3; the 3-month values printed are -0.25 and -0.34. SMDs are the standardized effects most likely to be extracted for meta-analysis, and the text uses them to characterize effects as small or modest. Confirmed, substantive, direct.

rows.R: Main p4 and Table 2 note d: NNT = 1/(difference in adjusted %). Recomputed all 81 NNT points in Table 2 and eTables 7-8 with +/-0.05 on each displayed %: every printed NNT equals the round-up (ceiling) of 1/RD, and 24 of 81 (including the 3 flagged) are incompatible with conventional rounding. Rounding NNT up is the standard convention and is applied consistently. Card names upward rounding as an alternative; my full-table check settles it.
rows.evidence: Main p4, p9 Table 2 (text layer and render); supp4 pp11, 14 eTables 7-8 (text). R script nnt.R. Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The three flagged points are severity 6-mo HC vs UC (37.1 - 22.9; 1/RD in [6.99, 7.09], printed 8), interference 6-mo HC vs UC (40.9 - 24.3; [5.99, 6.06], printed 7) and reminder-letter 6-mo PT vs UC (35.6 - 21.3; [6.94, 7.04], printed 8). Conventional rounding would give 7, 6 and 7. I recomputed all 81 NNT points in Table 2 (27), eTable 7 (18) and eTable 8 (27, plus negative NNH values), letting each displayed adjusted percentage vary by +/-0.05. Every printed point is attainable as ceiling(|1/RD|) with the sign of RD; 24 points, spread across all three tables, are attainable only by rounding up (e.g., pain intensity 3 mo PT vs UC 1/RD in [14.93, 15.38], printed 16; eTable 8 reminder 6 mo HC vs UC [5.15, 5.21], printed 6), and no printed point requires conventional rounding. The tables therefore apply the usual convention of rounding NNT up to the next whole number consistently. The footnote does not state the convention, but this is not a numerical error. Exclude.

rows.R: Protocol v5.0 PDF p56 (section 15.5) and SAP v6.0 p20 (14.0): adjust for baseline pain severity, sex, site, rural residence, multisite pain, mental health condition (no age). Main p4 gives the same list. Supp4 p4 and eTable 2 p7 call age part of the 'base set of pre-specified adjustment variables'; eTables 3-4 fit age >=65; xlsx eTable 3 G10 marks age as prespecified. Age was added to all primary models and described as prespecified. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Protocol supp1 PDF p56 and SAP supp2 p20 (encoded text; OCR and 110-dpi renders read visually); main p4; supp4 pp4, 7-9, 11, 14 (text); supp5 xlsx sheet eTable 3 (openpyxl). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: Both plan documents list the primary adjustment set as baseline pain severity, the stratification variables (sex, clinical site, rural/medically underserved residency) and the a priori predictors multisite pain and co-occurring mental health condition. SAP section 13 mentions age only as a descriptive and subgroup variable. The main article repeats the plan list. The results supplement, however, describes a 'base set of pre-specified adjustment variables: baseline pain severity, age, sex, ...', eTable 2 lists age (>=65 vs <65) among variables included in all models, the fitted models in eTables 3 and 4 include an age >=65 term (RR 1.15, 1.00-1.33), and the footnotes to eTables 7 and 8 list age. The xlsx flags age as a prespecified adjustment variable. The fitted primary model therefore includes a covariate that neither plan lists, and the main-text description of the adjustment set omits it. Covariate-set difference between plan and report; substantive_difference (descriptive). Not disclosed as a change.

rows.R: Protocol PDF p57 (section 15.6) and SAP p21 (section 15.0): secondary analyses 'follow the same approach as Aim 1' and 'include as covariates baseline levels of pain severity and all stratification variables'. Main p4: same structures 'with added adjustment for the given baseline secondary outcome'. The baseline value of each secondary outcome is an added covariate not in either plan. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Protocol supp1 PDF p57 and SAP supp2 p21 (OCR and renders read visually); main pp4, 10-11 (text). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: Both plans specify covariates for secondary analyses as baseline pain severity and all stratification variables, with a general statement that they follow the Aim 1 approach (which would import multisite pain and mental health condition). The report adds the baseline value of the given secondary outcome (for example baseline social role functioning for the social role model) and, through the 'same modeling structures', presumably also age, education and employment from the primary model. Adjusting for the baseline value of the outcome is a common and defensible choice, but it is not in either plan. How baseline adjustment applies to PGIC items, which have no baseline value, is not stated. Covariate-set difference; substantive_difference (descriptive only).

rows.R: SAP v6.0 (18 Jul 2024) p19 section 11: 'For the primary analyses, we will analyze those patients who have follow-up data' under MAR; if >15% missing or differential, pattern-mixture imputation plus IPW (IPW added by the 17 Jul 2024 amendment, p4, after follow-up ended Apr 2024) and worst/best-case sensitivity. Report (main p4; supp4 pp4-5, 11): weighted MNAR imputation is primary; complete-case labelled a 'pre-specified sensitivity analysis'. Disclosed (supp4 p5). The conditional clause can be read as authorizing the switch, so the plan's own hierarchy is ambiguous.
rows.evidence: SAP supp2 pp1-4, 19 (OCR; p19 render read visually); main p4; supp4 pp4-5, 9, 11 (text). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The only SAP supplied is version 6.0, dated 18 July 2024, after follow-up concluded in April 2024. Its section 11 first states that the primary analyses will use participants with follow-up data under a MAR assumption, then that missing data will be analysed and sensitivity analyses conducted 'as required (>15% missing at 3 months or differential missingness)', with a first approach (pattern-mixture imputation relaxing MAR plus inverse probability weights) and a second, explicitly sensitivity, approach (worst/best case). The change log (p4) shows IPW was added on 17 July 2024, with a statement that the biostatistician was masked to outcome data. The report treats the trigger as met (3-month completeness 77.1%) and makes the weighted MNAR analysis primary, and it calls the complete-case analysis a prespecified sensitivity analysis, a role the SAP does not assign. A difference in wording exists, and the IPW component was finalized after follow-up ended (disclosed, supp4 p5). Whether the analysis hierarchy itself differs depends on whether 'as required' applies to the primary analysis or only to sensitivity analyses, which the SAP does not settle. Retained, L indeterminate; disclosed.

rows.R: Main p9 Table 2: the six HC-vs-PT rows whose RR CI includes 1 (severity 6/12 mo, intensity 3/12 mo, interference 6/12 mo) print finite positive NNT CIs (e.g., 24 (12-186)), implying RD CIs above 0. In the text layer exactly these six use an en dash (U+2013) and all 21 others a hyphen. Reading the en dash as a lost minus (12 to -186) gives RD lower limits of -0.54, -1.32, -1.75, -2.63, -1.49, -1.27 points, matching those implied by the RR CIs (-0.66, -1.44, -1.70, -2.57, -1.48, -1.19) and footnote e. Printed intervals misstate null coverage. Beyond the card, which did not identify the mechanism.
rows.evidence: Main p9 Table 2 (text layer, character codes inspected; rendered at 170 dpi and read visually; table is printed rotated). R script nnt_sign.R. Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: Footnote e states that when the RD interval contains zero the NNT limits run from a positive lower limit to infinity and from a negative upper limit (NNH) to minus infinity; eTables 7 and 8 print such intervals with an explicit negative upper limit (e.g., 31 (13, -60)). In Table 2 the six HC vs painTRAINER rows whose RR interval includes 1 print NNT intervals of 24 (12-186), 41 (17-76), 37 (14-57), 63 (18-38), 26 (11-67) and 39 (16-79), which read as finite positive intervals and therefore as RD intervals excluding zero, contradicting the RR intervals and the text (no HC vs PT difference at 6 and 12 months). The text layer shows that exactly these six intervals use an en dash while every other interval in the table uses a hyphen. Interpreting the en dash as a minus sign lost in typesetting gives RD intervals [-1/U, 1/L]; the implied lower limits (-0.54, -1.32, -1.75, -2.63, -1.49 and -1.27 percentage points) agree closely with the lower RD limits implied by applying the RR limits to the painTRAINER percentage (-0.66, -1.44, -1.70, -2.57, -1.48, -1.19). The intended values are therefore 24 (12 to -186) and so on. As printed, the six intervals misrepresent null coverage for secondary HC vs PT comparisons; recovering the intended values requires this inference. Confirmed; substantive because the displayed intervals indicate a significant difference that the analysis did not find; downstream possible.

rows.R: Main p9 Table 2, pain intensity 12 mo HC vs PT: NNT 63 (18-38), point outside interval. 1/(33.7 - 32.1) = 62.5, so 63 is correct; RR 1.05 (0.92-1.20) includes 1. Same lost-minus mechanism as C008 (en dash): intended interval 18 to -38, i.e., RD -2.6 to 5.6 points. As printed the interval is impossible and also implies a significant RD.
rows.evidence: Main p9 Table 2 (text layer and render). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The point 63 lies above the printed upper limit 38. The point reproduces: 1/(0.337 - 0.321) = 62.5, rounded up to 63. The RR for the same contrast is 1.05 (0.92-1.20), so the RD interval must contain zero and the NNT interval must be of the 'NNT 18 to infinity / NNH 38 to infinity' type described in footnote e. The interval separator is an en dash, as in the five other affected rows (C008), consistent with a dropped minus sign; 18 to -38 corresponds to RD from -2.63 to 5.56 points, close to the RR-implied lower limit of -2.57. This row is one instance of the C008 error, recorded separately by the pipeline because the point falls outside the printed interval. Confirmed; coded substantive for consistency with C008 because the printed interval misstates null coverage, although the impossible interval makes the error visible to a careful reader.

rows.R: Main pp10-11 Table 3: I count 14 of 63 SMD points outside their printed 95% CIs (severity 12 mo PT/UC -0.25 (-0.24 to 0.01); physical 6 and 12 mo all three; PGIC pain 12 mo all three; etc.) and 18 intervals with reversed limits (all social and physical rows). Same root problem as C003 (SMD columns do not follow the stated construction). Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Main pp10-11 Table 3 (text layer, checked against render). R script smd.R. Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: Recomputed containment for all 63 SMD tuples: 14 points lie outside the numerical range of their intervals (severity 12 mo PT-UC and HC-UC; intensity 12 mo HC-UC; interference 12 mo PT-UC and HC-UC; physical 6 mo and 12 mo all three contrasts; PGIC pain 12 mo all three). Another 18 intervals are printed with the upper limit first (all social role and physical function rows). Several SMD intervals also disagree with the MD intervals on whether zero is excluded (21 tuples), which cannot happen if SMD = MD/SD with a fixed SD. These faults share the cause recorded under C003; the intervals cannot be used as printed. Confirmed, substantive, direct (SMD and CI are typical meta-analytic inputs).

rows.R: Supp4 p13 calls eTable 8 'the primary analysis restricting to subsets'; eTable 2 p7 and eTables 3-4 add education and employment to the primary imputation/estimation models. eTable 8 note b (p14) lists only sex, age, site, rural, multisite, mental health, baseline pain severity (copied from eTable 7, the complete-case analysis). Either the footnote is incomplete or the subset models are not the primary model. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp4, 7-9, 11, 13-14 (text). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The narrative describes eTable 8 as the primary analysis restricted to participants randomized after two protocol changes. The primary model includes education and employment selected by the stated procedure (eTable 2), as shown by the fitted coefficients in eTables 3 and 4. Footnote b of eTable 8 lists the base covariates only, identical to the eTable 7 footnote for the complete-case analysis, and also does not say whether imputation and weighting were applied. The description is internally inconsistent; which covariate set (and missing-data handling) was actually used cannot be determined. Probable rather than confirmed because 'primary analysis' may refer loosely to the modelling approach. Minor: sensitivity analyses whose conclusions are not affected by a two-covariate difference.

rows.R: Supp4 eTable 2 p7: additional weight-model predictors PEG, PHQ-8, GAD-7, any negative SDOH, education. Fitted weight model eTable 5 p10: PEG, PHQ-8, GAD-7, no negative SDOH, not employed; no education. xlsx eTable 3: education has no non-response P (I12 blank; H12 .0156, J12 .05), employment qualifies (H18 <.001, I18 .0228). eTable 5 matches the stated selection rule; eTable 2 names the wrong variable. Card agrees on the conflict; xlsx resolves which is right.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp5, 7, 10 (text); supp5 xlsx sheet eTable 3 rows 12-18, 39, 81, 84, 108 (openpyxl). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The stated rule (supp4 p5) adds a covariate to the weight model when it is associated at P < .10 with both 3-month MCID and any follow-up. In the xlsx, columns H (MCID) and I (overall non-response) give: PEG .0245/.0405, PHQ-8 <.001/.0095, GAD-7 .0327/.0331, any negative SDOH .0636/.0196, not employed <.001/.0228; education has H = .0156 but no non-response P (I12 blank; J12 = .05 refers to 3-month missingness). Under the rule the weight model should add PEG, PHQ-8, GAD-7, SDOH and employment, which is exactly what eTable 5 shows. eTable 2's final list names education instead of employment for the weight model. Confirmed labelling error in eTable 2; the fitted model appears correct. Minor.

rows.R: Supp4 eTable 2 p7: education selected as binary (any college vs HS or less). eTables 3-4 (pp8-9) show three education coefficients vs HS or less, two labelled 'AA degree' (e.g., eTable 4 RR 0.97 and 1.16). xlsx eTable 3 has four levels (HS or less, Associate's/Technical, College, Doctoral/Postgraduate), consistent with a 4-level term; the second 'AA' row is presumably College degree. Coding description and labels conflict. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp7-9 (text); supp5 xlsx eTable 3 A12:A16. Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: A binary education variable gives one coefficient; both fitted displays give three nonreference coefficients, which matches the four-category education variable in the xlsx. One of the two identically labelled 'AA degree' rows must be a different level; by order it is probably the college degree row (estimates rise with level: -0.02, 0.16, 0.39 in eTable 3; RR 0.97, 1.16, 1.35 in eTable 4), but this cannot be confirmed. The conflict between the stated binary coding and the fitted three-parameter term, and the duplicated label, are established. They concern adjustment covariates, not effect estimates; minor.

rows.R: Supp4 eTable 3 p8: across all 20 rows with exact P, the z implied by the CI is about 1.94 times the z implied by P (median ratio 1.94); printed P values match what each 'CI' would give if it were est +/- 1 SE (e.g., Pattern 2: 0.151 vs printed .150; Site 3: .070 vs .069). So the eTable 3 intervals are not 95% Wald intervals for the printed P values (likely +/-1 SE intervals, or P from a 1.96-fold SE). The three flagged ratio rows (eTable 4 age and second AA, eTable 5 PEG) reproduce within display rounding. Goes beyond the card on mechanism.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp4-5, 8-10 (text). R script etab345.R. Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: For eTable 3 (linear imputation model), I computed SE from each CI as width/3.92, the CI-implied z and P, and the z implied by the printed P. For every row with an exact P the ratio z_CI/z_P lies between 1.77 and 2.45 (median 1.94), with deviations explained by two-decimal rounding of small estimates; e.g., Time 6M 0.13 (0.07-0.19) gives CI-implied P = 2e-5 vs printed .025; Pattern 2 -0.28 (-0.47 to -0.08) gives .005 vs .150. Treating each printed interval as estimate +/- 1 SE reproduces the printed P values closely (Pattern 2 0.151 vs .150; Pattern 1 0.225 vs .226; Site 3 0.070 vs .069; second AA 0.075 vs .077; Male 0.0034 vs .003). A constant factor of about 1.96 is not what a different robust or joint variance estimator would produce (that would vary by coefficient), so the intervals or the P values in eTable 3 were computed with a misplaced critical value. Seven flagged eTable 3 rows are instances of this. The other three flagged rows reproduce: eTable 4 age 1.15 (1.00-1.33), CI-implied P .055 vs printed .046 and second AA 1.16 (1.00-1.33) .041 vs .046, eTable 5 PEG 0.96 (0.92-1.00) .055 vs .037; all are compatible once the limits printed as 1/1.00 are allowed their rounding range. Confirmed for eTable 3. These are coefficients of the step-1 imputation model, not effect estimates, so minor.

rows.R: Supp4 eTable 8 p14 first header: 'N=454; 366 with at least 1 follow-up; PT=149, HC=153, UC=152 at 3-months'. 149 + 153 + 152 = 454 = N randomized, exceeding 366. These are arm sizes, not 3-month counts; eTable 1 minus the post-enhancement block gives 3-month counts UC 109, PT 94, HC 108 (311). Other two headers are coherent (1487 <= 1670; 858 <= 935). Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp7, 13-14 (text). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The three arm counts sum exactly to the randomized N of the subset (454), and a count of 3-month completers cannot exceed the 366 participants with any follow-up. Subtracting the post-8/9/2021 3-month counts (UC 512, PT 448, HC 527) from the full-trial counts in eTable 1 (621, 542, 635) gives 109, 94 and 108 (total 311 <= 366), which are what the header label promises. The header therefore mislabels randomized arm sizes as 3-month counts. Both 454 = 149 + 153 + 152 and 454 + 1877 = 2331 reproduce. Label error in a sensitivity-analysis header; minor.

rows.R: Supp4 p15 calls eTable 11 'unadjusted mean' outcomes; p17 title/header say median (25th, 75th percentile). Most cells (e.g., social role 43.4 (42.8, 44.0)) are far too narrow to be IQRs of T-scores (SD about 7) and behave like means with 95% CIs; two PGIC cells (2.0 (1.0, 3.0); 2.0 (1.0, 2.0)) look like medians/IQRs. Beyond the card: in all 21 rows the three raw columns reproduce the printed MDs only if ordered UC, PT, HC (max deviation <= 0.1), not as labelled PT, HC, UC (deviations 0.6-3.3). Arm labels and statistic type are both wrong.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp15-18 (text; p17 rendered and checked). Main Table 3 pp10-11 for comparison. R script et11_cols.R. Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: Summary statistic: the narrative says means; the title and header say medians with 25th and 75th percentiles. For PROMIS T-scores with baseline SD 6-7 and 600+ participants per arm, bounds such as 42.8-44.0 cannot be quartiles; they match 95% CIs for a mean. Most PGIC cells (2.8 (2.7, 2.9)) are also CI-like, whereas the HC-labelled 3-month PGIC cells 2.0 (1.0, 3.0) and 2.0 (1.0, 2.0) look like integer medians with IQRs. Column order: I tested the printed between-group MDs against the raw columns. Under the printed labels (PT, HC, UC) the implied differences deviate by 0.6 to 3.3 units in every row (e.g., pain severity 3 mo: PT 5.1, UC 4.6, but PT-UC printed -0.5). Under the order UC, PT, HC every row reproduces all three MDs within 0.1 (21/21 rows). The ordering is also consistent with Table 3 (usual care improved least, so has the highest pain and lowest function). So the arm labels of the raw columns are permuted, and the two 'HC' PGIC cells that look like medians actually sit in the painTRAINER column. Anyone extracting arm-level follow-up summaries from eTable 11 would take the wrong statistic and the wrong arm. Confirmed, substantive, direct. The card raised the statistic-type conflict and explicitly did not infer an arm permutation.

rows.R: Supp5 xlsx sheet eTable 3, E82: 'Current depression (PHQ-8 >=10)' All Observed 711 (73.2); E3 N=1568, E83 missing 2; footnote A110: missing excluded from denominator. 711/1566 = 45.4%. Counts partition correctly (162 + 243 + 711 = 1116 = B82). Percentage wrong; count correct. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Supp5 xlsx sheet eTable 3 cells A82:E83, E3, A110 (openpyxl). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: 711/(1568 - 2) = 0.4540 (45.4%); printed 73.2%. The overall and other-group cells reproduce (1116/(2331 - 2) = 47.9%; 162/295 = 54.9%; 243/468 = 51.9%), and the counts sum to the overall total, so the count is correct and the percentage is a slip (a denominator of about 971 would be needed for 73.2%). The overall depression prevalence and the group contrast (higher in those with missing follow-up) are clear from the other cells. Minor.

rows.R: Supp4 eTable 11 p17, physical function: the covariance of the two UC contrasts is identified from the three contrast CIs (Cov = (v1 + v2 - v3)/2), so the 2-df Wald omnibus can be rebuilt without an independence assumption. Reconstructed P = .025 (6 mo; printed .005) and .010 (12 mo; printed .001); over the full rounding box the minimum is about .009 and .003, still above the printed values. 3-month (.18 vs .212) and social role rows reproduce. Both printed and rebuilt P are < .05, so the LSD gate is unchanged. Probable: assumes the omnibus used the same robust covariance as the contrasts. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp15, 17-18 (text; p17 render read); main p11 Table 3 note c. R scripts omni.R and omni_box.R (seed 20261014). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: With contrasts a = PT-UC, b = HC-UC and b - a = HC-PT from one model, Var(a), Var(b) and Var(b - a) determine Cov(a, b), so W = d' V^-1 d (2 df) is identified from the printed intervals. Physical function 6 mo: a = 1.1 (0.3-1.9), b = 0.4 (-0.3 to 1.1), HC-PT -0.6 (-1.4 to 0.1) gives W = 7.34, P = .025; 12 mo: 1.2 (0.4-2.0), 0.9 (0.0-1.8), -0.3 (-1.2 to 0.6) gives W = 9.18, P = .010. Sampling all inputs within +/-0.05 of their displayed values (50 000 draws, seed 20261014) gives minimum P of .0094 and .0032, still above the printed .005 and .001; the card's analytic bounds (.014 and .002) are similar. The same reconstruction reproduces the 3-month row (.18, range .09-.29, printed .212) and the social role rows (P < .001 or .001). The discrepancy holds under the stated Wald test with a shared covariance; it would disappear only if the omnibus test used a different variance estimator or model, which the footnote does not suggest. Given that eTable 11 also has mislabelled columns (C016), a production error is plausible. Probable issue; minor because both versions are below .05 and this is a supplementary unadjusted table.

rows.R: Main p3: PROMIS-29 has 7 domains (raw 4-20 each), higher scores better in some and worse in others. Main p6 and eTable 4 (supp3 p15) report one PROMIS-29 score (levodopa 66 (14) text, 64.74 (14.33) eTable 4; placebo 65 (14) / 65.11 (13.79)) and MD -0.37 (-3.34 to 2.61). No scoring rule, range or direction for this single score in the article, protocol (p70 v1.4 / OCR) or SAP. A sum of mixed-direction raw domains is not interpretable, and the sign of the MD cannot be read. Text 66 also does not round from 64.74. Card agrees; the text-table mismatch is additional.
rows.evidence: Main pp3, 6 (text); supp3 p15 eTable 4 (text); protocol supp1 p70 (OCR, 300 dpi); SAP supp2 p5 (OCR; no text layer). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The methods define PROMIS-29 as seven 4-item domains with raw scores of 4-20 and mixed direction (higher is better for physical function and social roles, worse for anxiety, depression, fatigue, sleep disturbance and pain interference), and pain intensity is a separate 0-10 item (protocol p70). The results nevertheless report a single PROMIS-29 mean per arm (about 65 in both groups, which is in the range of a raw sum of seven domains, 28-140) and an adjusted mean difference of -0.37. Neither the article, the protocol nor the SAP defines a PROMIS-29 total, its range, or whether any domains were reverse-scored, and PROMIS-29 has no standard total score (summary scores such as PROPr or physical/mental health summaries require a specified algorithm). The scale and direction of the reported outcome therefore cannot be identified, so the effect cannot be interpreted beyond 'no detectable difference' and cannot be extracted for pooling. In addition, the text gives the levodopa mean as 66 (14) whereas eTable 4 gives 64.74 (14.33), which rounds to 65; the placebo values agree. Confirmed reporting issue (undefined outcome scoring); substantive because the outcome measure itself is undefined for any downstream use; downstream possible (secondary, exploratory outcome).

rows.R: Protocol v1.4 (28 Feb 2023) p86 11.4.1: FAS = all randomized, ITT; 11.5: missing data by MI. SAP (signed 27 Sep 2024, after last visit 27 Aug 2024, before database closure 15 Oct 2024) p4 3.2 and footnote: deaths before visit 3 are in the FAS but contribute only to estimand 3 and the composite. Report p4: primary analysis excludes the 28 deaths (11 vs 17); n = 582. Death-inclusive estimands (3, 4, 10) are supportive. Partly disclosed (main p5: SAP differs from protocol in 'statistical terminology'). Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Protocol supp1 pp47 (cover v1.4), 86-87 (OCR and render); SAP supp2 pp1, 4, 6-7, 13 (OCR; p4 render); main pp2, 4-5, Figure 1; supp3 pp12-14 (text). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The protocol (both v1.1 p39 and v1.4 p86) defines the full analysis set as all randomized participants analysed by randomized group and handles missing primary data by multiple imputation, with no exclusion of deaths. The SAP, signed on 27 September 2024 (after the last participant's last visit on 27 August 2024 and before database closure on 15 October 2024), keeps the deceased in the FAS but states that they do not contribute to any analysis except treatment-policy strategy III and the composite (win ratio) strategy. The article's primary analysis follows the SAP and excludes the 28 participants who died before 3 months (11 levodopa, 17 placebo), giving 582 analysed (610 - 28 = 582; 307 - 11 = 296; 303 - 17 = 286, reproduced). Labelling this a 'treatment policy' estimand is itself questionable because death is handled by exclusion. Death-inclusive analyses (estimand 3, -0.98; win ratio 1.06; post hoc estimand 10 with FMA = 0 for deaths, -0.03) are reported as supportive and agree with the primary. Under the rule I applied to this year (a later plan finalized after follow-up ended does not supersede the protocol), the change of primary population is retained as a substantive difference. The article's statement that protocol and SAP differ in 'statistical terminology' understates it; partly disclosed.

rows.R: Protocol v1.4 p56 (synopsis) and p86 11.4.2: mixed model with baseline FMA, treatment and stroke type as fixed effects and a random intercept for center (v1.1 pp10, 39: same without stroke type). SAP p10 5.2, main p4 and code (supp5 lines 22-23: lm(FMA3 ~ baseline + medication), pooled by mice) fit baseline + treatment only. Center (a randomization stratum) and stroke type dropped. Not specifically disclosed. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: Protocol supp1 pp10, 39, 56, 86 (OCR; p86 render); SAP supp2 p10 (OCR); main pp3-4 (text); code supp5 p1 (text layer encoded; rendered at 150 dpi and read). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: Both protocol versions specify a mixed-effects model with a random intercept for center; v1.4 adds stroke type (ischemic vs hemorrhagic) as a fixed effect. The SAP (finalized after the last visit) specifies a linear model with baseline FMA and treatment only, and the published code fits exactly lm(fma_affected.Visit_3 ~ fma_affected.Visit_1.cent + medication) on each imputed data set. Randomization used center-stratified minimization, so omitting center from the analysis model departs both from the protocol and from the usual practice of adjusting for stratification factors; stroke type was also prespecified in the final protocol. With center imbalance minimized the point estimate may change little, but the standard error and the estimand of the planned model are not reported. The article's general statement about protocol-SAP differences in terminology does not cover this model change. Substantive difference in the primary model (descriptive).

rows.R: SAP p11 section 6: missing secondary outcomes imputed as for the primary (100 MICE imputations); only harm outcomes not imputed. Main p5: mRS and PRAI missing data not imputed; supp3 p7 lists these as SAP deviations (deaths set to mRS 6; PRAI not imputed). eTable 4: mRS n = 596, PRAI n = 546 vs 582 for other secondaries. Disclosed (supp3 p7). Card agrees.
rows.evidence: SAP supp2 p11 (OCR and render); main p5 (text); supp3 pp7, 15 (text). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The SAP applies multiple imputation to all secondary outcomes other than harm outcomes. The report did not impute the mRS or the patient-reported assessment of relevance of motor improvement: deceased participants were assigned mRS 6 (the scale's definition of death, which is reasonable) and missing PRAI responses were left missing, giving analysis sets of 596 and 546 rather than the 582 used for the other secondary outcomes. Whether surviving participants with missing mRS were imputed or dropped is not stated; the main text's blanket statement is broader than the supplement's death-only explanation. The supplement discloses both as deviations from the SAP. Retained as a disclosed difference in missing-data handling for two secondary outcomes. Also noted: the PRAI placebo numerator is 52/270 in the text (p6) but 51/270 (18.89%) in eTable 4.

rows.R: SAP p12 7.2 and addendum pp14-15 (4 Oct 2024): 7 prespecified subgroup interactions (age, sex, distal motor function, cortical dysfunction, SSRI, stroke type, baseline FMA <median vs >=median) in a forest plot; SAP p11: center and treatment-by-center terms in the main model; protocol v1.4 p86 11.4.3: stroke-type interaction and covariate-adjusted sensitivity analyses. None is reported (supp3 index p1; eFigure 7 p27 shows only post hoc PH1-PH3). Report labels the FMA <=35/>35 subgroup and the center plot post hoc, although the plan prespecified a median split (median 34) and the center display. Main p5 says prespecified analyses were performed as outlined. Card agrees.
rows.evidence: SAP supp2 pp11-12, 14-15 (OCR; p11 render); protocol supp1 p86 (render); main pp4-5, 7 (text); supp3 pp1, 18, 25, 27 (text; eFigures 5, 7 and eTables 7-8 rendered at 100 dpi). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: The SAP prespecifies seven subgroup analyses of the primary estimand, each with a subgroup-by-treatment interaction and presented as a forest plot, with directional hypotheses recorded in the ICEMAN addendum dated 4 October 2024 (before database closure). It also specifies a model including center and a treatment-by-center interaction, and the final protocol adds a treatment-by-stroke-type interaction and covariate-adjusted sensitivity analyses (age, sex, dementia, hand/wrist movement, cortical dysfunction, fatigue, SSRI, extrapyramidal symptoms, impetus). The supplied report contains none of these results: the supplement index lists estimand tables, a continuous baseline-FMA interaction and spline model (eTables 7-8, post hoc), a center boxplot (eFigure 5, called post hoc in the article although the protocol and SAP prespecified a graphical display by center) and a post hoc forest plot with two estimands and one baseline-FMA subgroup (<=35 vs >35). The last is close to the prespecified baseline-severity subgroup (overall median 34) but uses a fixed cut point and is labelled post hoc. The article states that prespecified analyses were performed as outlined in the SAP. Planned subgroup and center analyses of the primary outcome are not reported; retained as a substantive difference. The complete-case (estimand 2) and per-protocol-type analyses (estimands 6, 7; PH2) are reported, so the omission concerns the subgroup, interaction and covariate analyses.

rows.R: Main p6 Table 2 (rendered): levodopa top-level SAE categories sum to 143 vs parent 126; placebo 139 vs 129. Infection subtypes sum to 59 vs 55 (levodopa) and 52 vs 44 (placebo). Stroke (15+1, 18+1) and cardiac (5+5+2, 1+2+0) subtypes reconcile; AEs of interest reconcile (79, 67). No note says an event may count in several categories, and 'Other (none of the above)' implies exclusive coding. Counts are integers, so rounding does not apply; all four comparisons fail, not only the two the card registered.
rows.evidence: Main pp6-7 (text; Table 2 rendered at 200 dpi to check indentation); supp3 pp16-17 eTables 5-6 (text). Card read after judgment.
rows.rationale: Recomputed: levodopa 55+16+5+12+4+4+6+3+3+2+1+0+32 = 143 vs 126 events; placebo 44+19+10+3+7+5+2+6+4+2+3+0+34 = 139 vs 129. Infection subtypes: levodopa 27+15+5+0+1+11 = 59 vs 55; placebo 17+15+7+2+2+9 = 52 vs 44. Subtypes of stroke and cardiac events add exactly to their parents, and the prespecified AEs of interest add exactly to 79 and 67, so the table is otherwise additive. The rendered table indents only the stroke subtypes; cardiac subtypes, 'Fall', 'Fracture' and 'Traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage' are printed at the category level, which makes the hierarchy itself ambiguous (Trauma 4 = Fall 4). An event with several diagnoses or infection sites could be counted in more than one category, which would explain sums above the parent totals, but the table does not say so, and the card's precision allowance of +/-0.5 per summand is not appropriate for integer counts. The arm totals (126, 129; eTable 5 n = 255) and infection totals (55, 44) are consistent with the text, so the overall SAE picture is clear; the category breakdown cannot be reconciled as printed. Probable issue (multiple coding unstated), minor, downstream possible for category-level harms extraction. eTable 6 also gives n = 145 overall for prespecified AEs vs 67 + 79 = 146 (outside this candidate).
